Paul Klee, a Swiss-German painter and pedagogue whose whimsical, experimental approach to color, line, and form made him one of the twentieth century's most inventive artists.

Born in Bern, Klee trained as a musician, and music's compositional logic informed his approach to visual form. He worked across abstraction, Surrealism, and figuration, creating a visual language of infinite playfulness: childlike symbols, hieroglyphic marks, and prismatic color harmonies.

Klee joined the Bauhaus in nineteen twenty-one and taught there until its closure by the Nazis in nineteen thirty-three. His courses became legendary. He developed what he called taking a line for a walk—the idea that a line's path could be playful, intuitive, and liberating. He used transparent watercolor and oil transfer techniques to layer color, creating luminous surfaces of ethereal beauty.

Klee systematized color theory for students: primary color relationships, warm and cool contrasts, and color as emotional carrier in visual communication. His teaching revolutionized art education by systematizing color and form into teachable principles. He taught students not what to paint but how to see, how to think through materials and composition.

Klee fled Nazi Germany in nineteen thirty-three and spent his final years in Bern, increasingly abstract and political. He created thousands of works throughout his life; his prolific output combined high seriousness with a spirit of playful experimentation. His work merged musical structure with visual form, treating paintings as compositions where color, line, and space interacted like notes in musical harmony.

Generations of students learned from him at the Bauhaus, becoming carriers of his revolutionary methods. His approach—systematic yet playful, rigorously intellectual yet visually joyful—established the school as the twentieth century's greatest design laboratory.
